questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
Tests basic security posture enforcement in manifests, a real-world gate that beginners can implement with standard policy engines.

## Key Concepts
- container securityContext: runAsNonRoot, readOnlyRootFilesystem, capabilities (drop ALL)
- privileged flag handling
- policy engines: Kyverno, OPA Gatekeeper

## Code Example
```yaml
# Kyverno policy (minimal)
apiVersion: kyverno.io/v1
kind: ClusterPolicy
metadata:
  name: require-secctx
spec:
  rules:
  - name: check-security
    match:
      resources:
        kinds: ["Deployment", "StatefulSet", "DaemonSet", "Pod"]
    validate:
      message: "Containers must set runAsNonRoot, readOnlyRootFilesystem, and drop ALL capabilities"
      pattern:
        spec:
          template:
            spec:
              containers:
              - securityContext:
                  runAsNonRoot: true
                  readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
                  capabilities:
                    drop: ["ALL"]
```

```yaml
# Failing manifest (no securityContext, privileged)
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: foo
spec:
  replicas: 1
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: app
        image: nginx:latest
        securityContext:
          privileged: true
```

```yaml
# Passing manifest (proper securityContext)
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: bar
spec:
  replicas: 1
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: app
        image: nginx:1.21
        securityContext:
          runAsNonRoot: true
          readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
          capabilities:
            drop: ["ALL"]
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you adapt the gate for multi-tenant clusters with namespace-scoped policies?
- What would you test locally to avoid CI regressions?

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
Multi-tenant clusters need strict API access control; SPIFFE identity ensures only trusted services can perform sensitive calls. Gatekeeper + OPA enforces runtime policy with centralized visibility.

## Key Concepts
- OPA Gatekeeper
- ConstraintTemplate and Constraint
- SPIFFE IDs and SVIDs
- Kubernetes API verbs and RBAC implications
- Validation via audit logs and Gatekeeper status

## Code Example
```yaml
# ConstraintTemplate
apiVersion: templates.gatekeeper.sh/v1beta1
kind: ConstraintTemplate
metadata:
  name: k8sapicnst
spec:
  crd:
    spec:
      names:
        kind: K8sApiConstraint
  targets:
    - target: admission.k8s.gatekeeper.sh/v1beta1
      rego: |
        package k8sapi
        violation[{"msg": msg}] {
          input.review.kind.kind == "Pod"
          input.review.object.metadata.namespace != "monitoring"
          not allowed_spiffe(input.review.object)
          msg := sprintf("Pod %s in namespace %s cannot use API verb %s", [input.review.object.metadata.name, input.review.object.metadata.namespace, input.review.operation])
        }
        allowed_spiffe(pod) {
          pod.metadata.annotations["spiffe.io/spiffe-id"]
          pod.metadata.annotations["spiffe.io/spiffe-id"] in data.constraint.spec.allowedSVIDs
        }
```

```yaml
# Constraint
apiVersion: constraints.gatekeeper.sh/v1beta1
kind: K8sApiConstraint
metadata:
  name: restrict-api-verbs
spec:
  enforcementAction: deny
  allowedSVIDs:
    - "spiffe://ibm.com/workload/web"
    - "spiffe://tesla.com/workload/monitor"
    - "spiffe://cloudflare.com/workload/edge"
```

## Validation Plan
1. Deploy ConstraintTemplate and Constraint
2. Test compliant GET request from approved SPIFFE ID
3. Test noncompliant POST request from unapproved SPIFFE ID
4. Verify denial in Gatekeeper audit logs
5. Confirm monitoring namespace bypass works correctly

## Why This Is Asked
Tests ability to enforce secure secret handling across multi-cloud clusters, using policy-as-code, and integrating cert-manager with GitOps pipelines.

## Key Concepts
- Policy as code (Kyverno/OPA)
- cert-manager Certificate -> Secret flow
- ExternalSecret / SecretStore integration
- CI gating and canary verification

## Code Example
```yaml
# Kyverno policy (example)
apiVersion: kyverno.io/v1
kind: ClusterPolicy
metadata:
  name: deny-inline-tls-and-enforce-secretref
spec:
  validationFailureAction: fail
  rules:
  - name: deny-inline-tls
    match:
      resources:
        kinds: ["Deployment", "StatefulSet"]
    validate:
      message: "TLS data must come from cert-manager SecretRef; do not inline certificates"
      pattern:
        spec:
          template:
            spec:
              volumes:
              - secret:
                  secretName: "?!*"
```

```rego
# OPA/ValidatingAdmissionPolicy (illustrative)
package kubernetes.admission

deny[{"msg":"inline certs not allowed"}] {
  input.request.kind.kind == "Deployment" or input.request.kind.kind == "StatefulSet"
  some i
  secret := input.request.object.spec.template.spec.volumes[i]
  secret.secretName != "" # ensure SecretRef used, not inline data
}
```

```yaml
# Failing manifest (inline cert example)
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: tls-secret
type: kubernetes.io/tls
data:
  tls.crt: LS0tLS1CRUdJTiBDRVJUSUZJQ0FURS0tLS0t... # inline cert data
  tls.key: LS0tLS1CRUdJTiBSU0EgUFJ...
```

```yaml
# Passing manifest (SecretRef to cert-manager Secret)
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      volumes:
      - name: tls
        secret:
          secretName: my-cert-manager-secret
```

```yaml
# CI validation steps (high level)
- lint manifests
- run policy gate (Kyverno/OPA) on PR
- validate that Deployment references cert-manager Secret (no inline data)
- run a quick canary test in a staging cluster
```

- How would you test this in a mono-repo with many teams?

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked

This question tests foundational secure supply chain practices in a beginner-friendly manner. It mirrors real-world CI gates used in production environments around Dockerfile hygiene, image signing, SBOM generation, and registry controls. It introduces modern tools like Cosign and SBOM attestations without overwhelming complexity.

## Key Concepts

- **Dockerfile Hygiene**: Non-root USER and multi-stage builds reduce security vulnerabilities and image size
- **Container Image Signing**: Using Cosign to sign and verify container images ensures integrity
- **SBOM Attestation**: Software Bill of Materials provides transparency into image contents and dependencies
- **GitHub Actions Workflows**: Implementing gates and policy checks in CI/CD pipelines
- **Registry Allowlist**: Restricting deployments to approved registries prevents supply chain attacks

## Code Example

```yaml
# Minimal GitHub Actions workflow
name: Docker Security Gate
on: [push, pull_request]

jobs:
  gate:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      
      - name: Validate Dockerfile
        run: |
          # Check for non-root USER
          grep -q 'USER ' Dockerfile || exit 1
          # Check for multi-stage build
          grep -q 'FROM.*AS' Dockerfile || exit 1
      
      - name: Build and push image
        run: |
          docker build -t ${{ vars.REGISTRY }}/app:${{ github.sha }} .
          docker push ${{ vars.REGISTRY }}/app:${{ github.sha }}
      
      - name: Generate SBOM
        run: |
          syft ${{ vars.REGISTRY }}/app:${{ github.sha }} -o spdx-json > sbom.json
      
      - name: Sign image and SBOM with Cosign
        run: |
          cosign sign ${{ vars.REGISTRY }}/app:${{ github.sha }}
          cosign attest --type spdx-json --predicate sbom.json ${{ vars.REGISTRY }}/app:${{ github.sha }}
      
      - name: Verify signature and attestation
        run: |
          cosign verify ${{ vars.REGISTRY }}/app:${{ github.sha }}
```

## Why This Is Asked
This question tests end-to-end security design for multi-cloud Kubernetes workloads, focusing on identity, secret management, and policy enforcement with real-world tools.

## Key Concepts
- Zero-trust workload identity (SPIRE)
- Ephemeral credentials (Vault)
- Service mesh security (Istio, mTLS, AuthorizationPolicies)
- Policy-as-code (OPA/Rego)
- Egress controls to data lake and namespace isolation

## Sample Solution

### 1. SPIRE Workload Identity
```yaml
# spire-workload.yaml
apiVersion: spire.spiffe.io/v1alpha1
kind: ClusterSPIFFEID
metadata:
  name: data-platform-workload
spec:
  names:
    - data-service
    - analytics-service
    - etl-service
  namespaceSelector:
    matchLabels:
      environment: production
```

### 2. Vault Integration for Secrets
```yaml
# vault-secret-store.yaml
apiVersion: secrets.hashicorp.com/v1beta1
kind: VaultSecret
metadata:
  name: data-lake-credentials
  namespace: data-platform
spec:
  vaultAddress: https://vault.data-platform.svc.cluster.local:8200
  path: secret/data-lake
  provider: hcp
  refreshInterval: 1h
```

### 3. Istio AuthorizationPolicy
```yaml
# istio-authz.yaml
apiVersion: security.istio.io/v1beta1
kind: AuthorizationPolicy
metadata:
  name: data-lake-access
  namespace: data-platform
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: data-lake-gateway
  rules:
  - from:
    - source:
        principals: ["spiffe://data-platform/data-service"]
    to:
    - operation:
        methods: ["GET", "POST"]
        paths: ["/v1/tables/*"]
```

### 4. OPA Policy Example
```rego
#.rego
package kubernetes.admission

deny[msg] {
  input.request.kind.kind == "Pod"
  input.request.namespace == "restricted"
  not input.request.object.spec.securityContext.runAsNonRoot
  msg = "Pods must run as non-root"
}

allow[msg] {
  input.request.kind.kind == "Deployment"
  input.request.object.spec.template.spec.containers[_].securityContext.privileged
  msg = "Privileged containers not allowed"
}
```

### 5. CI Enforcement Check
```yaml
# .github/workflows/security-scan.yml
name: Security Scan
on: [push, pull_request]
jobs:
  opa-check:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Run OPA policy check
        run: |
          opa eval --fail-defined-deny \
            --data policy.rego \
            --input manifests/
```

## Key Takeaways
- SPIRE provides cryptographically secure workload identity
- Vault enables dynamic secret rotation without application changes
- Istio mTLS ensures service-to-service encryption
- OPA/Rego enforces admission control and runtime policies
